stories.text: Ibuprofen was first made at Boots in Nottingham in December 1961, by Stewart Adams's team. Their later laboratory, on Pennyfoot Street, is now BioCity, and in 2013 a Royal Society of Chemistry blue plaque marked the discovery. Adams and the chemist John Nicholson filed the patent in 1961; the drug was first sold in Britain in 1969, as Brufen, and in 1983 it became the first such painkiller apart from aspirin sold over the counter in the UK.[^ibu]
In 1837 the present church was built to Thomas Rickman's design. Between 1909 and 1912 it was extended to designs by George Frederick Bodley.

300343.sum: St Stephen's Church, Sneinton is a parish church in the Church of England. It is the parish church of the Sneinton suburb of Nottingham, Nottinghamshire, England. The church is Grade II listed by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport as it is a building of special architectural or historic interest.

stories.text: William Booth, who founded the Salvation Army, was born in Sneinton on 10 April 1829. At 13 he was apprenticed to a pawnbroker. His birthplace is now a museum.

William Booth, who founded the Salvation Army, was born in this house in Notintone Place, Sneinton. It is now the William Booth Birthplace Museum, telling the story of Booth, his wife Catherine and their family.
William Booth Birthplace Museum opened in 1971. Subject: personality: religious.

300350.sum: William Booth's birthplace. Today it houses The William Booth Birthplace Museum. The building dates from about 1820, according to Historic England (via Wikipedia). It is Grade II listed as William Booth Memorial Social Centre.

stories.text: Shortly after 1807 the baker George Green built a tower mill here. It burned in 1947, was restored and reopened in 1986, and is now part of a science centre.
George Green, the mathematician, was a miller: his family's windmill in Sneinton is restored and named after him.[^s1] He was a member of the subscription library at Bromley House.[^s1][^s2]

300387.sum: Green's Windmill is a restored and working 19th-century tower windmill in Sneinton, Nottingham. Built in the early 1800s for the milling of wheat into flour, it remained in use until the 1860s. It was renovated in the 1980s and is now part of a science centre, which together have become a local tourist attraction.
